mainTopic: Who cancels the vows of a נערה המאורסה (a betrothed young woman): her father, her ארוס, or both together? Here the גמרא tests each option against the פסוקים.
overview: The גמרא first finishes showing that the פסוק 'ואם היו תהיה לאיש' is about a betrothed woman, and it adds a second proof: the word 'הויה' means קידושין. Next it asks who cancels her vows. Maybe the father can cancel alone? No. The Torah would then not need to say that he cancels when she is not betrothed. Maybe the ארוס can cancel alone, and the father is mentioned only to teach that his confirming the vow holds? No. Then the פסוק 'בית אישה נדרה' about a married husband would be extra, since a קל וחומר would teach it. The challenger replies that this פסוק teaches that a husband cannot cancel vows made before the marriage. But that means the ארוס can cancel such earlier vows, which even a married husband cannot do. The גמרא explains this: the ארוס's power comes from his partnership with the father. So for a נערה המאורסה, both must cancel together.

steps.title: Don't we already know this on our own?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back on the earlier reasoning. It says the conclusion follows automatically from another פסוק, so the earlier argument was not needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: But don't you learn it automatically from it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא objects to the reasoning it just used to show that the פסוק is about a betrothed woman. It says we would know this anyway, without that argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק 'ואם בית אישה נדרה' already covers a fully married woman. So the other פסוק must be about a betrothed woman, and we can figure that out by ourselves. The earlier argument therefore adds nothing, and the גמרא needs a different way to show the point.

keyTerms.meaning: automatically, by itself
you learn from it
but isn't it so that... (an opening for a challenge)

phrases.english: But don't [you] automatically
phrases.notes: He means: from the פסוק 'ואם בית אישה נדרה' (במדבר 30:11), which already covers a married woman.

phrases.english: learn it from it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the previous derivation (from before this section) as unnecessary.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the method of the earlier proof, not its conclusion that the פסוק is about a betrothed woman.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The argument proves something we would already know from the פסוק of 'בית אישה'.

steps.title: The word 'being' means betrothal
steps.stepSummary: A second way to show the פסוק is about a betrothed woman: the word 'הויה' ('to be' to a man) means קידושין.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or if you want, say that the word 'being' [to a man] means betrothal.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new, cleaner proof that 'ואם היו תהיה לאיש' is about a betrothed woman. The wording itself shows it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'to be to a man' (הויה) is the Torah's language for קידושין, not for full marriage. So the פסוק is directly about a נערה המאורסה, and we don't need the argument that was just rejected.

keyTerms.meaning: if you want, say... (introduces another answer)
'being' (to a man); taken from the word 'תהיה' in the פסוק
betrothal, the first stage of marriage
means, implies

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the whole topic that follows: the פסוק is about a betrothed woman, so the question is who cancels her vows.

phrases.english: Or if you want, say:
that 'being' [to a man] means betrothal.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the proof that was just rejected with a word-based proof.
steps.raayaObject: That the פסוק of 'ואם היו תהיה לאיש' is about a betrothed woman.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The word 'הויה' in the פסוק, which means קידושין.

steps.title: Maybe the father cancels alone
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that maybe the father can cancel his betrothed daughter's vows all by himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: Say that the father cancels by himself!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא puts a new idea on the table: perhaps the ארוס is not needed, and the father alone cancels. This sets up the next step, which answers it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This challenges the rule that the father and the ארוס cancel together. If the father had full power on his own, the ארוס would play no role at all.

keyTerms.meaning: say (that maybe...)
father
by himself, alone
cancels (a vow)

phrases.english: Say that the father cancels by himself!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Now that the פסוק is set as being about a betrothed woman, the גמרא asks who cancels her vows.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that the father and the ארוס cancel together.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Maybe the father's power alone is enough, even when she is betrothed.

steps.title: Then why would the Torah say the father cancels in his own house?
steps.stepSummary: The idea is rejected. If the father cancels alone even when there is an ארוס, the Torah would not need to say he cancels when there is no ארוס.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why do I need 'and she binds a bond in her father's house... he disallows her'? Now, if you could say that when there is an ארוס the father cancels by himself, is it necessary [to say so] when there is no ארוס?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the suggestion from the previous step. The Torah's separate teaching about a girl in her father's house would be pointless.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah tells us that a father cancels the vows of his daughter at home, when she is not betrothed. If he could cancel alone even when she is betrothed, then obviously he could when she is not, and the פסוק would be extra. So the father alone cannot cancel once she is betrothed.

keyTerms.meaning: if so
he will disallow, meaning cancel
why do I need it?
the man she is betrothed to
is it necessary [to say]?

steps.confusionAlert: 'במקום ארוס' does not mean 'in place of' the ארוס. It means 'where there is an ארוס', that is, when she is betrothed.

phrases.english: If so, 'and she binds a bond in her father's house',
'he disallows her', why do I need it?
Now, if one could say
that where there is an ארוס, the father cancels by himself,
is it necessary [to say so] where there is no ארוס?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם כֵּן ״וְאָסְרָה אִסָּר בֵּית אָבִיהָ״ ״יָנִיא אוֹתָהּ״ לְמָה לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the suggestion that the father alone cancels.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A פסוק would be extra (a קל וחומר shows it would be unneeded).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The father might cancel his betrothed daughter's vows alone.
steps.terutzMaskana: The Torah's separate teaching about the unbetrothed girl shows that once she is betrothed, the father cannot cancel alone.

steps.title: Maybe the ארוס cancels alone, and the father matters only for confirming
steps.stepSummary: A new suggestion: the father needs the ארוס, but the ארוס can cancel alone. The challenger also heads off the reply 'then why mention the father?' He says the father is mentioned only to teach that if the father confirms the vow, it stays confirmed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Say that the father needs the ארוס, but the ארוס cancels by himself. And if you say: why do I need the father whom the Torah wrote? It is needed [to teach] that if he confirmed, it is confirmed!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests the opposite idea: maybe only the ארוס has full power. It even answers ahead of time the obvious reply, so the challenge stays strong. The next step answers it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 4 showed the father cannot act alone, but that doesn't prove the ארוס can't. The usual proof that both are needed is that the Torah mentions the father. The challenger says that mention could serve a different purpose: to teach that the father's confirming (הקמה) blocks the ארוס from cancelling.

keyTerms.meaning: needs, requires
and if you say... (heading off an expected answer)
the Merciful One, meaning the Torah
confirmed (the vow), so it can no longer be cancelled

phrases.english: Say that the father needs the ארוס,
but the ארוס cancels by himself.
And if you say:
the father whom the Torah wrote, why do I need him?
phrases.notes: He means the Torah's mention of the father in the section about a betrothed girl.

phrases.english: It is needed [to teach] that if he confirmed, it is confirmed!
phrases.notes: Once the father confirms the vow, the ארוס can no longer cancel it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵימָא אָב לִיבְעֵי אָרוּס, וְאָרוּס לְחוֹדֵיהּ מֵיפֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After ruling out 'father alone', the גמרא tests 'ארוס alone'.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that the ארוס cannot cancel without the father.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The Torah's mention of the father could be explained by the father's power to confirm, so it doesn't prove his cancelling is required alongside the ארוס.

steps.title: Why would the Torah need to mention the married husband?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the idea that the ארוס cancels alone. If that were true, the פסוק about a married woman's husband would teach nothing new, because we could learn it with a קל וחומר.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why did the Torah write 'she vowed in her husband's house'? It is a קל וחומר: if the ארוס cancels alone even while the father still has a say, then surely the husband cancels alone once the father has no say. Why would we need a פסוק for that?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the suggestion from Step 5. It says the ארוס cannot cancel alone, because then the Torah's words about a married husband would be extra.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 5 said the ארוס can cancel by himself. The גמרא replies that a married husband is clearly stronger than an ארוס, because the father is no longer involved. So if the weaker ארוס cancels alone, the stronger husband surely does, and the פסוק 'בית אישה נדרה' would be unnecessary.

keyTerms.meaning: A logical argument: if a rule applies in the weaker case, it surely applies in the stronger case
'Her husband's house', meaning a fully married woman
When the father still has a say, as during אירוסין
By himself, alone

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'without the father' means a married woman. Once she is married, her father no longer has any say over her vows.

phrases.english: If so,
phrases.notes: He means: if the ארוס really can cancel by himself, as Step 5 suggested.

phrases.english: "She vowed in her husband's house": why was it written?
It is a קל וחומר:
If where the father still has a say
the betrothed man cancels by himself,
where the father has no say, is it even a question?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם כֵּן, ״בֵּית אִישָׁהּ נָדָרָה״ לְמַאי כְּתִב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects Step 5's claim that the ארוס can cancel alone.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing that a פסוק would be extra (מיותר) using a קל וחומר
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ארוס cancels alone, and the father only has the power to confirm the vow.
steps.terutzMaskana: That cannot be right, because then 'בית אישה נדרה' would be extra.

steps.title: Maybe the פסוק teaches about vows made before the marriage
steps.stepSummary: The challenger saves his idea. He says the פסוק about the husband's house is not extra. It teaches that a husband cannot cancel vows his wife made before they were married.
steps.simpleTranslation: Say that 'And if she vowed in her husband's house' comes to teach that the husband cannot cancel vows she made earlier.
steps.whatsHappening: The challenger gives the 'extra' פסוק a new job, so he can keep his idea that the ארוס cancels alone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 6 said the פסוק would teach nothing. Now the challenger reads it closely: 'in her husband's house' means only vows she made while married. So a husband cannot cancel vows from before. If the פסוק has its own lesson, the argument from Step 6 falls away.

keyTerms.meaning: Say, maybe we can say
Earlier vows, made before the marriage
Husband, here meaning a fully married husband

phrases.english: Say: "And if she vowed in her husband's house"
comes to teach that the husband does not cancel earlier vows!
phrases.notes: Earlier vows are ones she made before she married him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defends Step 5 by finding a new purpose for the פסוק that Step 6 called extra.
steps.kashyaTarget: Step 6's claim that 'בית אישה נדרה' would be extra
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק is needed for a different lesson, that a husband cannot cancel vows made before the marriage. So it is not extra.

steps.title: Then the ארוס would be stronger than the husband
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows where this reading leads. If only the married husband is limited, the ארוס alone could cancel earlier vows. That makes no sense.
steps.simpleTranslation: And from that, it would follow that the ארוס does cancel earlier vows!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out what follows from Step 7's reading: the ארוס would be able to cancel vows made before the betrothal, even though a married husband cannot. That is surprising, and the next step explains it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the פסוק limits only the married husband, then the ארוס could cancel vows from before the betrothal. But a married husband has more power over his wife than an ארוס, so why would the ארוס have this extra power on his own? That would make no sense if he acted alone. It only makes sense if his power comes from somewhere else, and Step 9 says it comes from his partnership with the father.

keyTerms.meaning: And from it, meaning from that same reading

phrases.english: And from it: the betrothed man cancels earlier vows.
phrases.notes: Read it with surprise: this would make the ארוס stronger than a married husband, unless his power comes from somewhere else. The next line explains where.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Refutes Step 7 by showing its reading leads to an unacceptable result.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reductio: following the idea to its end shows it cannot be right
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק only stops the married husband from canceling earlier vows.
steps.terutzMaskana: Then the ארוס could cancel earlier vows and seem stronger than the husband. That is unreasonable if he acts alone, and it is resolved in Step 9 by his partnership with the father.

steps.title: The ארוס cancels only as the father's partner
steps.stepSummary: Since every other option has failed, the גמרא concludes that the ארוס has no power to cancel alone. He cancels only together with the father, as his partner.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, isn't it because of his partnership with the father?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws the final conclusion of this discussion: the ארוס's power to cancel comes only from his partnership with the father.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 8 showed that the ארוס can cancel vows from before the betrothal, which even a married husband cannot do. The only way to explain this is that his power is not his own: he works as the father's partner, and the father can cancel all her vows. So the ארוס cannot cancel alone, and together with Step 4 (the father cannot cancel alone either), both must cancel together.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, isn't it...? This is how the גמרא brings a conclusion
Partnership

steps.whatToRemember: For a נערה המאורסה, neither the father nor the ארוס can cancel her vows alone. The ארוס cancels only as the father's partner, so both must cancel together.
steps.whyThisMatters: This explains the rule in the משנה that the father and the ארוס together cancel the vows of a betrothed girl.

phrases.english: Rather, isn't it because of his partnership with the father?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion now that the 'ארוס alone' option has been ruled out.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The ארוס cancels his betrothed's vows only in partnership with the father, never alone.
